Based on my analysis:

**Test image observations:**
- Dried/straw-colored corn husks (narrow, elongated, fibrous) collected in a black bag
- Uniformly tan/straw colored — no green remaining, no visible mold growth
- Background shows a mature corn field (late season)
- No leaf lesion patterns, no rust pustules, no dark spore masses

**Key comparisons:**
- **Ear_rots_Diplodia**: Top reference panels show straw/bleached husks still on plant — very characteristic premature husk bleaching. Closely matches the uniformly straw-colored husk material in the test image
- **Fusarium**: Shows straw-colored husks too, but with white-pink mold on kernels; lower-left panel similar but not as clean a bleach
- **Diplodia stalk rot**: Shows dried stalk material scattered on ground — different context
- **Northern corn leaf blight / Gray leaf spot**: Active green leaves with tan lesions — doesn't match dried material
- **Ear_rots_Gibberella**: Dark/black staining on husks — not matching the clean straw color

The material appears to be collected corn husks showing the characteristic premature bleaching associated with Diplodia ear rot — the husks lose color and dry prematurely while still on the plant, producing this uniform straw/tan appearance without other distinctive mold colors.
